records.title: Emergency Department-Initiated Buprenorphine for Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
records.source_title: Emergency Department-Initiated Buprenorphine for Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
records.abstract: PubMed abstract verified against the primary record. In a multicenter randomized trial across 29 US emergency departments, 1994 unique adults with untreated opioid use disorder were analyzed after assignment to 7-day extended-release injectable buprenorphine or sublingual buprenorphine. Seven-day and 30-day treatment engagement were similar between groups. Precipitated withdrawal was uncommon in both groups despite frequent fentanyl exposure; overdose events through 30 days were equal between groups. Several secondary outcomes favored extended-release treatment, including craving, recent illicit opioid-use days, and satisfaction.
records.relevance_reason: Direct human randomized evidence on emergency-department buprenorphine initiation, withdrawal safety, fentanyl-era applicability, overdose outcomes, and short-term treatment engagement.

study_details.primary_outcome: engagement in opioid use disorder treatment at day 7

population.description: Adults presenting to US emergency departments with untreated opioid use disorder and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale score of 4 or higher

intervention.comparator: sublingual buprenorphine with 7-day prescription for 16 mg/day

outcomes: Day-7 treatment engagement: 40.5% extended-release vs 38.5% sublingual; adjusted difference 1.6 percentage points, 95% CI -2.8 to 6.0
Day-30 engagement was similar between groups
Overdose events within 30 days: 2.3% in each group
Secondary craving, illicit-opioid-use-day, and treatment-satisfaction measures favored extended-release treatment

uncertainty.primary_outcome: No detected superiority for day-7 treatment engagement; confidence interval includes clinically meaningful benefit and harm
uncertainty.secondary_outcomes: Some secondary outcomes favored extended-release treatment and should not be generalized beyond the studied emergency-department population and regimen

adverse_effects.overdose_30_days: Equal observed proportion in both groups

interactions.drug_drug_interactions: Not a primary objective of this trial

limitations.duration: Primary comparative follow-up was short term
limitations.generalizability: Findings apply to the studied formulations, dosing protocols, eligibility criteria, and referral pathway

provenance.verification_note: Title, identifiers, design, participant counts, primary and secondary outcomes, safety outcomes, and abstract were checked against the PubMed record.
